english: When something ends up happening the opposite way it was supposed to.
notes: Often used as a shorthand for 'the other way around' in some contexts.
description: It refers to when the opposite of something happens. For example, if you said 'Subuthu hahaen konin ẽ payaru payawanoãieji. Subĩ nasũ ninru ana?' (I wanted to play through the day and study near the time for the exam. I should be able to pass, right?), but failed, then you could say that the apple ate the human. Another example: you devise a plan, pretending to be children; however, when the plan is executed, everyone thinks you're grown men. The apple ate the human! It can also be used as an alternative for 'inside-out,' like 'kamumai ryōe atora ji' (feed this to the apple), which can mean 'turn this inside-out' or 'make it the other way around,' depending on context.

literal: Brain of apple / An apple for a brain
english: When someone is being extremely idiotic or acting creepy or perverted.
notes: Extremely vulgar, since 'apple' here refers to a boob.
description: If someone says something creepy or weird, you would use this, like in 'so ni atora no riwakango;' however, since this phrase is quite harsh and vulgar, it often is better not to say it, unless the context allows for it.

english: To signal that you're free or to tell someone to wait.
notes: Usually paired with the germane imperative or request marker.
description: Use 'au chisun aiko' in respectful and formal contexts, 'ake au chisun' to signal immediacy or annoyance, like saying 'enough!' and use 'fuka' for a simple request, like 'please, wait.' This is the standard phrase for wait / hold it / one second / you have me (to you). You can also use it in moments like, 'wait a minute... something seems off.' it attention, a potential change in stance, and even disbelief.

notes: Paired with particles like 'yad' or a tired tone.
description: This is the stereotypical idiomatic expression for when a project fails, something goes wrong, or when you 'give up.'

english: Asking the other person to be gentle, calm, or more patient.
notes: Needs to be paired with the germane mood particle.
description: Used to ask others to calm down, relax, or take a breather. It must be used with the proper mood particle (e.g., ake, aiko, or fuka) depending on politeness and if its a command or request. It can also be used to mean 'stop,' especially in favour of 'have my water' if you don't want the other nuance.

english: Telling someone you've got their back.
notes: Use the romantic form in relationships or for highly intimate commitments. Romantic form (annyu instead of au) can't be used and should not be used casually.
description: Should be constructed with an omitted pronoun or the proper pronoun / referent particle based on context.

english: Admitting an error or expressing anger at oneself.
notes: Can be mildly vulgar in some contexts, especially when paired with the interjection à.
description: It is like exclaiming 'shit,' 'damn,' or 'my bad' in English. It can be used to admit an error ('namekosun, iireu ei' - my bad, will fix that/make it better) or to express frustation or anger at oneself: 'eeeehhh, namekosun!' (arghh, my mistake / that's on me)

phrase: Makure a rrahwo i shi riwakasarunai
ipa: makuɺe a ɾahʷo ʔi ɕi̥ ɺiwəkasaɺunai
gloss: trial A NEG-essence COP COND think-PERF.RES-MID
literal: Trials are negated if always thinking
english: Your endurance means nothing if you're constantly overthinking
notes: Very poetic, literary, and solemn. 'makure' is often marked with the person, like 'makurezun' (your endurance). Makure is a hard word to translate, but it means something like 'painful sobs from one's inner self.'
description: It's like saying 'even a patient man has a limit' or 'if you keep overthinking, there will be a time when your patience runs and you give up / do something you regret.'

Instead of (...), an often absurd sentence is made, the most common one being 'hiroga o bakaiǵ' (the world is flat). It's like saying, 'I could be thinking that the world is flat, but X is strictly forbidden.' For example, 'su ni hiroga o bakaiǵ, hashiru ni hahaen sōe ieji ga errasaru inai' (I could think that the world is flat, but the children playing near him will never be okay).

literal: My gut feels full of water / water
notes: A polite phrase to reject drinks or food.
description: Instead of direct rejection, it is better to use this. In terms of illness, you would use 'ochi a, ngopo o aishinai!' (the bloating is really hurting my gut!), but there are a million ways to communicate that. Do note that amgkantei is not used for genuine pain or illness, unless it was the food that made you ill (e.g., in cases of food poisoning). Bloating is the universal Tawish metaphor for stomachaches.

literal: Rising above only to be put back down
english: The ups and downs of life
description: In English, we would say, 'sometimes, life is good, sometimes it isn't.' In Tawa, you say, 'ujute unai.' It is used similarly to other languages' forms of expressing 'life has its ups and downs.'

notes: Refers to someone who does not take care of their physical hygiene or are unhealthy.
description: It can be quite rude but using it in forms like 'hyakoson ga rrai lilingu ue, riwakanai' (to me, it seems / I think (that) his clothes are not his size) for someone who is fat is usually more polite.

literal: Mutilated into convenient servings my heart
notes: The feeling here is objectification, like being 'hollowed out.' Used for heartbreak and severe betrayal. Often followed with 'oto, ya?' (I'm bewildered / how was it so casual?) or other appropriate particles. The romantic particles would make it non-serious, so it is best unmarked or if absolutely necessary (which it often never is), marked with -ru (which carries 'vulnerably/nakedly' as a connotation). With -nyu (romantically) on himae (himaenyu - romantically mutilate), it makes it feel more like a sitcom or performative, instead of serious heartbreak.
description: It is an extremely visceral idiom. You'll see it in sentences like: 'mātasēoisun ga himaetenai nukōe no makure... oto, ya?' which is like saying 'the person that was going to be the love of my life mutilated the inner wails (of pain) of my heart into convenient servings (for dinner), and I'm bewildered as to how casual they were about it.' Here, -tenai marks the implied purposive (for dinner). It makes the would-be love of their life (mātasēoisun) feel like a total psychopath. You can also just say 'himaenatenai' if you're really tired.

notes: The feeling here is visceral torture. You are 'knotted up.' Esace is a very taboo word due to its severity, so use with extreme care. Romantic form is usually never used (same reason with the mutilation idiom).
description: This is used for tragedies of cruelty. It isn't a simple 'broke my heart' cliché. It's an almost-taboo-level idiom. It's like saying someone took your will to live or destroyed your ability to process emotions, since ngopo is the centre of processing in Tawa. It is where you 'feed' yourself - both food and metaphorically beliefs. If you restrain and train it, you will be disciplined, otherwise it will consume you and make you a spiteful person. This is why ngopo is used in this idiom, and also why it is almost a taboo to use it (because it is literally the twisting of the engine of processing). The short form used is esacerai or the archaic esacerunai.
